newsitem.title: UK: British utility Eurobonds braced for budget.
newsitem.headline: British utility Eurobonds braced for budget.

text.p: Spreads on sterling Eurobonds issued by British utilities remained firm ahead of Wednesday's budget, despite underperforming the rest of the market in expectation of a windfall tax.
"All the utility spreads have been relatively volatile over the past month," Societe Generale Eurobond analyst Tom Rayner said.
"Over the last two weeks there's been a general tightening of spreads across the Eurosterling market but utilities have tended to lag the rest," he added.

Utility sterling bonds have traded more expensively than similarly rated companies in other sectors in expectation that Britain's Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown will levy a tax against privatised British water and electricity companies in his first budget on Wednesday.

The so-called windfall tax is expected to raise between three and five billion sterling. It is still unclear whether the tax will be faced by other large privatised companies such as British Telecommunications Plc and British Airports Authority Plc.
The tax has been priced into Eurobond spreads and these are unlikely to move on Wednesday unless the levy is larger than expected, bankers said.
"The tax has been pretty well-flagged over the last few months and, barring any increase in the tax, most things are factored in at the moment," a Eurosterling trader said.
There is a question whether the tax could result in credit downgrades for utility companies.
"Most of the companies have made provisions and are very strong financially so it would take a servere hit from the budget before the credit quality comes into question," Rayner said.

Last week three regional electricity companies were downgraded by European rating agency IBCA. London Electricity, Yorkshire Electricity, and East Midlands Electricity were lowered after acquisitions.
"The IBCA downgrades highlights that there are risks from the utility sector and we're telling people in general to avoid utility debt," a trader said.
British utility companies have been active borrowers in the sterling Eurobond market.

A benchmark for the sector is an issue by Eastern Electricity, a unit of Energy Group. The 8.75 percent 2012 bond was last week trading at a bid offer spread of 92/90 basis points, compared with a spread of 87/85 b.p. on Tuesday.
"It's an interesting area for someone who has a strong view for what's going to be in the budget," another analyst said.
